claims.text: A calibrated molecular-dynamics framework using machine-learned interatomic potentials and thermodynamic integration can predict melting temperatures of high-entropy alloys within approximately ±10% of experiment.
The proposed framework can predict fusion enthalpies of high-entropy alloys within approximately ±10% of experiment.
The proposed framework can predict fusion entropies of high-entropy alloys within approximately ±10% of experiment.
The proposed framework can predict volume changes at melting for high-entropy alloys within approximately ±10% of experiment.
The proposed framework can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys within approximately ±10% of experiment.
A machine-learned potential trained on representative high-entropy-alloy configurations can provide a detailed representation of interatomic interactions.
The machine-learned potential is anticipated to capture local atomic-environment effects.
The machine-learned potential is anticipated to capture many-body interactions.
Accurate reproduction of atomic interactions enables molecular-dynamics simulations to capture complex melting-transition dynamics.
Thermodynamic integration can efficiently calculate the free-energy change associated with melting.
Melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change can be derived from the calculated phase thermodynamics.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be obtained from equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations.
The claimed accuracy applies to compositions within the well-sampled compositional domain of the potential's training set.
Traditional classical empirical potentials often deviate from experiment more than the proposed approach.
First-principles calculations are generally too computationally expensive for application across a wide high-entropy-alloy compositional space.
Prediction accuracy may deteriorate for compositions substantially different from the potential's training compositions.
Prediction accuracy may deteriorate when long-range interactions are especially important.
Extreme compositional or structural inhomogeneity and rare atomic configurations may limit prediction accuracy for liquid properties and phase transitions.
The approach is to be falsified if predictions differ from experiment by more than ±10% for at least 80% of tested alloys within the intended compositional range.
